<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    The term
                    <jats:italic>data sovereignty</jats:italic>
                    —the principle that data is subject to the laws and governance of the country where it is collected or stored—faces implementation challenges. The legal deadlock over how to regulate transatlantic (E.U.–U.S.) data transfers reveal the difficulties of asserting “sovereignty” over data, a resource that flows transnationally through digital technologies. Among global regulatory efforts, the European Union’s struggle to ensure the supremacy of its data protection and privacy laws represents an interesting case from which to derive new theoretical and conceptual insights. This paper advances
                    <jats:italic>data agency</jats:italic>
                    —as agency mediated
                    <jats:italic>by</jats:italic>
                    data, not
                    <jats:italic>over</jats:italic>
                    it. The intention is to advance a term that moves beyond the limits of data sovereignty to explain how governance over data-driven systems is distributed and contested. The manuscript suggests pragmatic pathways for more effective governance as mere “control” over data is not enough to achieve meaningful insights derived from data technologies.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>The exponential shift of global foreign direct investment toward digital infrastructure prompts host states to enforce stringent screening mechanisms and data localization policies to safeguard critical national security interests. However, these sovereign assertions inevitably clash with international investment law. Using a comprehensive doctrinal legal method through statutory, conceptual, and comparative approaches, this study examines the tension between digital sovereignty and investment protections. The results indicate that mandatory data localization and post-establishment cybersecurity interventions significantly breach Fair and Equitable Treatment standards and constitute indirect expropriation, exposing host states to massive international investor-state dispute settlement claims. Consequently, this research concludes that developing jurisdictions, particularly Indonesia, must urgently reconstruct their bilateral investment treaties. By systematically integrating specific digital security exceptions, strictly redefining intangible digital assets, implementing proportional risk-based screening, and guaranteeing independent administrative due process, host states can effectively mitigate arbitration risks while securely facilitating global digital economic market integration and data sovereignty.</jats:p>
title: Foreign Investment in Digital Infrastructure: State Control, Risk Mitigation, and Data Sovereignty

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This article examines the future of the world economy from the standpoint of middle powers, with particular attention to Canada in the wake of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s renewed emphasis on middle-power coordination. It argues that the central economic transformation is not simply digitization, but a deeper pivot from the production of goods and knowledge toward the valuation of data generated through those production processes. Agriculture, manufacturing, health, education, logistics, and public administration are increasingly organized around data capture, platform intermediation, and AI-enabled recombination. This shift intensifies economies of scale, network effects, and economies of scope, thereby concentrating economic power in a small group of multinational technology firms. For middle powers, the resulting challenge is not to reject global platforms, but to avoid operational dependency on them. The article advances digital sovereignty as a framework based on control, interoperability, public-interest data governance, sovereign compute, and contestable digital markets. It concludes that middle powers must develop the state as a platform: a provider of trusted digital foundations that can sustain innovation, democratic accountability, and strategic autonomy in an increasingly platformized world economy.</jats:p>
title: Middle powers in the platform economy: Digital sovereignty after the data pivot

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper aims to advance an original intersubjective framework for data sovereignty governance. Grounded in constructivist concepts of shared understanding and critical realist principles of structure and agency, it moves beyond state-centric models to develop the concept of “interactive data sovereignty.” The study thereby offers a more robust theoretical and practical pathway for rebalancing power among states, platforms and individuals, contributing to a more equitable and effective global data governance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This paper uses a conceptual-theoretical methodology rooted in intersubjective and structural analysis. The approach reconstructs data sovereignty through an intersubjective lens, shifting it from a state-centric attribute to a relational status formed through multi-actor communication. It then integrates this perspective with a structural analysis of how power embeds within data architectures. The synthesis of these two lenses directly informs the interactive data sovereignty framework, deriving its core principles – interactivity, relativity and justice – and positioning data architecture as the central governance object.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study reveals that governance of data architecture fundamentally shapes power relations in dataspace. The proposed model of interactive data sovereignty demonstrates how participatory mechanisms can rebalance asymmetric relationships, with multilateral institutionalized consultations emerging as the most effective approach for reconciling data circulation and protection imperatives. This framework successfully bridges theoretical insights with practical governance solutions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study pioneers the integration of intersubjectivity theory with data sovereignty, proposing the novel concept of interactive data sovereignty. It innovatively identifies data architecture as the core governance object and develops participatory architecture as practical solution, offering new theoretical frameworks for rebalancing digital power disparities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Governing dataspace through intersubjectivity: from exclusive control to interactive data sovereignty

items.abstract: <jats:p>Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have become pivotal in a wide range of applications due to their high mobility, broad coverage, and multi-sensor integration. Advances in wireless networks have further spurred interest in cross-domain collaboration among UAVs from diverse institutions, platforms, and control domains, giving rise to decentralized federated sensing as an emerging research direction. However, the absence of trusted intermediaries, dynamic network topologies, and heterogeneous data ownership make it challenging to achieve ownership-controllable and fine-grained data protection in such decentralized UAV networks. To tackle these challenges, we first propose a blockchain-based decentralized access control framework for UAV federated sensing networks. We then devise a Hybrid Data Token Model (HDTM) along with an Unspent Fungible Token Outputs (UFTO) mechanism, which enables UAVs to encode their data into digital tokens and establish composable and traceable token usage records on the blockchain. Building on this foundation, a scalable Smart-contract-driven Attribute-Based Access Control (ScaBAC) algorithm is further developed to automate data token transfer decisions in a fully decentralized manner, supporting flexible, fine-grained, and auditable control over UAV data sharing. Experimental results on Hyperledger Fabric demonstrate that the proposed scheme achieves favorable throughput, reduced latency, and enhanced security compared to conventional ABAC and BCAC models, validating its practicality for real-world deployment.</jats:p>
title: How Do UAVs Govern Data Sovereignty in Decentralized Federated Sensing Networks? Tokenized Access Control via Policy-Driven Smart Contracts

items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper is a doctrinal rejoinder to the Inniss Data Nullius Framework (Inniss, 2025), which proposes a "Principle of Data Reversion" under which rights over data generated within a territorial jurisdiction would revert by default to the state or the generating collective, drawing on the colonial repudiation tradition of Mabo v Queensland (No 2) [1992] HCA 23. The paper accepts the political-economic diagnosis but argues that the framework's doctrinal architecture cannot stand against the Caribbean constitutional and statutory record it does not engage.<br><br>Three failures are identified. First, the locus of sovereignty. Julian Robinson v Attorney General [2019] JMFC Full 04 has already allocated informational privacy to the individual citizen under section 13(3)(j) of the Jamaican Charter; the state is duty-bearer, not right-holder. Second, the diagnosis. The Caribbean Court of Justice in Nervais &amp; Severin v The Queen [2018] CCJ 19 (AJ) has rejected the "frozen at independence" portrait on which the framework's institutional vacancy claim rests. Third, the remedy. Data reversion to the state reproduces the vacancy fiction it claims to repudiate, and the Mabo lineage, properly read, supports the citizen's prior right against state appropriation, not state appropriation against platform extraction.<br><br>The paper proposes a Three Locks operational counter-doctrine — Law, Function, Contract — anchored in the Data Protection Act, 2020 and the supply-chain reality that determines whether constitutional sovereignty is preserved or surrendered.</jats:p>
title: Sovereignty Allocated, Not Asserted A Jamaican Rejoinder to the Inniss Data Nullius Framework

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
          <jats:p>Digital value chains require the exchange of data. This data is always sensitive in one way or another—whether due to data protection, trade secret protection, or the very individual protection needs of data providers and data consumers along the value chain. It is therefore important to preserve the data sovereignty of all parties involved in the value creation. This requires three solution blocks, which we address in this article: (1) offering user-friendly ways to express data sovereignty needs and understanding their consequences; (2) devising technologies to enforce these needs; and (3) providing infrastructure in the form of digital platforms and their special form, data trustees, to enable a trustworthy data exchange between all involved parties.</jats:p>
title: Concepts for Data Sovereignty in Digital Value Chains: Data Cockpits—Data Usage Control—Data Trustees

items.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter addresses that analytical fragmentation by developing a comparative framework through which localization rules, AI governance instruments, and sovereignty claims are examined as mutually conditioning layers of digital statecraft rather than as isolated legal categories. A structured review of an uploaded Scopus corpus, which contained 139 records, was combined with a comparative analysis of India, Indonesia, Kenya, and Brazil, alongside official instruments issued by the African Union, UNESCO, the OECD, and NIST. The analysis demonstrates that broad territorial restrictions on data do not by themselves produce operational digital sovereignty; durable sovereignty is achieved when selective localization is aligned with data classification, compute and cloud capacity, risk-based AI governance, and interoperable cross-border transfer mechanisms.</jats:p>
title: Data Localization, AI Governance, and Digital Sovereignty in Emerging Economies

items.abstract: <jats:p>The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), quantum computing, and cybersecurity is transforming digital systems into cognitive infrastructures that increasingly mediate governance, economic coordination, and societal trust in the digital economy. While existing governance frameworks address AI ethics, quantum security, and digital sovereignty as separate policy domains, no sufficiently integrated model currently explains how their convergence reshapes technological power, institutional autonomy, and regulatory capacity — particularly for economies in the Global South.This paper addresses that gap through two contributions. First, it introduces cognitive sovereignty — defined as the capacity of a society to design, control, interpret, and govern the intelligent systems that shape collective decision-making, security, and trust. Unlike digital sovereignty, which centres on data ownership and infrastructural control, cognitive sovereignty directs analytical and policy attention toward governance of algorithmic logic, machine-mediated cognition, and quantum-classical computing architectures. Second, the paper develops the Cognitive Infrastructure Model (CIM), a four-layer diagnostic framework comprising computational intelligence, security architecture, governance systems, and societal processes. The CIM identifies specific misalignment conditions across these layers and derives targeted policy responses. The framework is applied analytically to India, diagnosing its position as a case of high governance ambition combined with moderate computational autonomy and significant external security dependency — a condition the model identifies as “regulatory theatre” risk.The paper contributes an integrated policy framework for understanding and governing sovereign AI–quantum ecosystems, with direct implications for ICT regulation, digital economy governance, and technology policy in both advanced and emerging economies.</jats:p>
title: Governing Cognitive Infrastructures: A Policy Framework for AI–Quantum Sovereignty in the Digital Economy

items.abstract: <jats:p>As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes value-laden societal outcomes worldwide, the imperative for robust governance has become critical. Yet the global AI governance literature remains disproportionately Western-centric, frequently overlooking the structural and infrastructural realities of Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). This paper bridges the gap between theoretical critique and practical implementation by proposing a Five-Pillar AI Governance Framework tailored to SSA. The framework is substantiated through a qualitative documentary analysis of contemporary African policy developments, employing a most-different systems comparative design across the divergent regulatory pathways of Rwanda, Nigeria, and the African Union. Policy evidence is extracted and coded against three governance indicators - infrastructural sovereignty, stakeholder participation, and institutional enforcement - and mapped onto the proposed structural pillars to produce an operational governance matrix. The resulting architectural blueprint offers African policymakers a practical roadmap for harnessing AI safely while safeguarding local digital sovereignty.</jats:p>
title: Decolonizing Digital Sovereignty: An Operational Framework and Policy Analysis of AI Governance in&nbsp;Sub-Saharan Africa

items.abstract: <jats:p>As smart energy systems become central to national sustainability strategies, ensuring data sovereignty—the right of nations to control data generated within their borders—has become a pressing priority. Yet, most current AI infrastructures lack built-in mechanisms for jurisdictional compliance, data localization, and legal accountability. This study explores how Artificial Intelligence (AI) can actively enforce data sovereignty within smart grid environments through a comparative analysis of four international cases: Gaia-X (EU), Microsoft’s EU Data Boundary, a decentralized energy pilot in India, and Saudi Arabia’s NEOM. Using expert interviews and document analysis, the paper investigates the role of federated learning, edge AI, and sovereign cloud architectures in aligning technical solutions with national governance goals. The study proposes a cross-jurisdictional framework for sovereign-by-design AI systems, highlighting ethical, legal, and infrastructural components. Results show that AI can be a powerful enabler of sovereignty—if supported by localized infrastructure, clear legal frameworks, and ethical oversight. The paper contributes original insights and a practical blueprint for policy-makers, developers, and energy stakeholders aiming to build compliant, ethical, and sustainable digital infrastructure aligned with global SDG targets.</jats:p>
title: Empowering Data Sovereignty Through Artificial Intelligence: A Framework for Sustainable Smart Energy Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>The impact of economic agreements on Indigenous peoples’ broader rights and interests has been subject to ongoing scrutiny. Technological developments and an increasing emphasis on Indigenous sovereignty within the digital domain have given rise to a global Indigenous data sovereignty movement, surfacing concerns about how international economic law impacts Indigenous peoples’ sovereignty over their data. This Article examines the policy space certain governments have reserved under international economic agreements to introduce measures for protecting Indigenous data or digital sovereignty (IDS). We argue that treaty countries have secured, under recent international digital trade chapters and agreements, the benefits of a comprehensive economic treaty and sufficient regulatory autonomy to protect Indigenous data sovereignty.</jats:p>
title: Protecting Policy Space for Indigenous Data Sovereignty Under International Digital Trade Law

items.abstract: <jats:p>"Sovereign AI" has become one of the most heavily used and least disciplined terms in contemporary technology policy. Governments fund it, vendors claim it, and journalists report it, but the word is applied indiscriminately to at least five distinct properties-the provenance of a model, the location of its training compute, the origin and control of its data, the jurisdiction of its deployment, and the nationality of the company selling it-which can vary independently of one another. This paper introduces the Sovereignty Stack, a layered diagnostic instrument for assessing any product marketed as "sovereign" AI. It operationalises the state-theoretic framework developed across the author's prior work on political visibility, sovereign AI, cognitive sovereignty, state capability, infrastructural politics, and the epistemic conditions of AI governance (Chow 2026a-g), turning a set of conceptual distinctions into a procedure a non-specialist-a procurement official, a regulator, a journalist-can run. The framework rests on three principles: sovereignty is not additive and cannot be reduced to a single score; control, exposure and jurisdiction are distinct and must not be conflated (a dependency is not the same as a loss of sovereignty); and a vendor's claim and the verifiable reality are separate measurements, so that the exercise is as much a claim audit as a sovereignty assessment. Its central analytical device is a provenance gate: base-model provenance (Layer 2) determines whether a model can be classified as lineage-sovereign, while training-data sovereignty (Layer 3) qualifies that classification; both stand analytically upstream of operational sovereignty (Layers 4 and 5), while compute (Layer 1) is recorded as an infrastructure-exposure variable rather than a classification gate-because provenance fixes what the model is while infrastructure only determines where and under whose authority it operates. The framework further distinguishes the object of a sovereignty claim-the sovereignty of the model from the sovereignty of the AI capabilityand supplies a veto-point criterion for when a dependency crosses from exposure into loss of sovereignty. The paper specifies the architecture, a due-diligence questionnaire (Appendix A), an evidence-and-date scheme with an evidential-asymmetry rule, a product-level typology, and a worked assessment card (Appendix B), and illustrates the method on anonymised current UK products. The core claim can be stated compactly: sovereignty is not a property of a company, a cloud region, or a deployment environment; it is a time-indexed property of an artefact's lineage and operation, assessed layer by layer against the jurisdiction making the claim.</jats:p>
title: The Sovereignty Stack: A Layered Framework for Assessing Sovereign-AI Claims - From Model Provenance to Operational Control

items.abstract: <jats:p>Over time, data has replaced oil as the central resource around which narratives of African development revolve., and yet the leading data-generating economies in Africa have remarkably little control over where such data will reside, by whom it will be processed and under what legal terms and conditions it may leave national territory. Nigeria, Africa's largest digital market by user base, illustrates this paradox acutely: a domestic data protection statute of considerable technical sophistication sits atop an infrastructure landscape still overwhelmingly dependent on foreign-owned cloud platforms, undersea cables, and hyperscale data centres. This paper probes the notion of data sovereignty for the Nigerian digital economy, theoretically distinguishes it from conceptually cognate (yet not coterminous) data localisation, data protection, and digital sovereignty. It provides a critique of the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 and the earlier regulation governing cross border data transfer within the EU's GDPR; India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023; and China's framework on data security; analyzes the supranational regulatory space constituted by the Malabo Convention, the AU Data Policy Framework, and the recently adopted AfCFTA Protocol on digital Trade; argues that Nigeria’s failure to ratify the Malabo Convention reflects a larger lack of intra-continental consensus for collective bargaining with global technology companies. The paper ultimately argues that data sovereignty, properly conceived, is neither an act of digital autarky nor exclusively a claim of territorial dominion over the digital realm, rather, it represents an essential project of institution building: Nigeria lacks neither the technical or legal capacity for the regime but that it requires-institutionally credible regulators; selectively targeted localisation of strategically important categories of data; and active cooperation with other African Union states toward common legal frameworks-rather than a maximalist embrace of territoriality that risks economic disadvantage. It concludes with targeted recommendations for the NDPA; the National Assembly and AU bodies.</jats:p>
title: <p>Data Sovereignty in Africa: Building A Sustainable Framework for Cross-Border Data Governance in Nigeria's Digital Economy</p>

                  <jats:p>This study explores the factors influencing national security effectiveness by examining structure and functionality, interagency coordination, policy alignment, and democratic governance. It also identifies key areas for improvement. The aim is to evaluate how these elements impact national security outcomes. The study surveyed 470 officials across the Palace of Justice, achieving a 78% response rate. Using SPSS (Statistical Package for the Social Sciences), the study demonstrates that structure and functionality, interagency coordination, policy alignment, and democratic governance significantly impact national security. It further shows that improvements in key areas have a substantial positive effect. items.abstract: <jats:p>This paper demonstrates that Canadian Hansard, which represents an exact transcript of the debates conducted in the House of Commons of Canada, is a valuable source for analyzing political positions on Arctic sovereignty using the Narrative Policy Framework (NPF). Unlike sporadic official documents, Hansard offers a continuous empirical dataset. While our research supports the NPF postulates, it proposes a complementary methodological approach through a Canadian narrative case study. Our findings suggest that MPs’ narratives align with those in official governmental publications and policy frameworks, reflecting the NPF’s primacy of groups and networks and narrative cognition postulates. Even though small to moderate lexicon differences were found in debates on Canadian Arctic sovereignty among the political parties, we observed a consistent lexicon across political affiliations. The period analysis demonstrated that Conservative MPs’ narratives align with what is expected based on NPF postulates. However, the policy reorientation in terms of beliefs, values, and norms caused by the Northern Strategy in conjunction with wavering leadership and unclear Arctic priorities created internal inconsistencies within the Liberal and New Democratic Party (NDP) narratives. These observations suggest that MPs’ narratives are more ambiguous than initially assumed, since they can deviate from official documents or publications because of current events before reverting to their core preferences. This study underscores the potential for continual empirical analysis of Hansard and the NPF’s applicability in Canadian policy studies.</jats:p>
title: Canadian Hansard and Arctic Sovereignty: A Narrative Policy Framework Study

items.abstract: <jats:p>The exponential growth of data has turned transnational data governance into a strategic priority for global data hubs. While the concept of “data as the new oil” highlights big data’s economic value, the dominance of large technology firms and increasing geopolitical tensions have prompted states, particularly China, to assert stronger control over cross‐border data flows. Since the 2016 Cybersecurity Law, China’s legislative approach has evolved significantly, culminating in comprehensive frameworks such as the Personal Information Protection Law and the Data Security Law. While prior research has focused on China’s legal infrastructure and data localization mandates, this study examines the adaptive and geopolitical dimensions of its transnational data governance strategy—an area that remains underexplored. Drawing on a content analysis of central‐level legislation from 2016 to 2024, this study identifies shifting legislative priorities, governance mechanisms, and legal rationales. The findings show that China has developed a multi‐layered and increasingly flexible legal regime that balances sovereignty claims with selective openness, reflecting a pragmatic response to domestic needs and international pressures. This study expands the original scope of the “Beijing effect” by showing that China’s influence on global data governance extends beyond the export of digital infrastructure to include dynamic legal adaptation and strategic regulatory innovation.</jats:p>
title: Adaptive Sovereignty: China’s Evolving Legislative Framework for Transnational Data Governance

items.abstract: <jats:p>Brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) have moved out of the laboratory and to clinics, rehabilitation centres, and wearable electronics faster than the legal instruments meant to govern them. Global BCI-focused venture funding roughly tripled between 2024 and 2025, and market estimates for 2025 range from just above two billion to nearly three billion US dollars, depending on the analytical firm and device categories counted [2], [3]. None of this growth has been matched by settled legal category for the data these devices produce. Neural signals are still processed, in most jurisdictions, as a subtype of health or biometric data, which misses what actually makes them different: they are a direct, largely involuntary readout of cognitive and affective states that the person generating them cannot fully control or even consciously monitor. This paper treats that gap as the central problem. We review the current state of dataprotection law as it applies (or fails to apply) to neural signals, examine the recently adopted UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology [1] as the first international soft-law instrument in this space, and propose NeuroGuard, a three-layer framework that pairs a legal definition of “neuro-sensitive data” with a technical architecture for consent-aware encryption and a STRIDE-based threat model adapted to BCI signal pipelines. We also introduce a scoring instrument, the Cognitive Sovereignty Index, intended as a starting point for comparing how completely a jurisdiction or product protects neural data and signals across legal, technical, and governance dimensions. The paper closes by naming what the framework does not yet solve, since a proposal at this stage is better judged on its stated limits than on a claim to completeness.</jats:p>
title: NeuroGuard: A Cognitive Sovereignty Framework for Neural Data Protection in Brain–Computer Interfaces

items.abstract: <jats:p>The notion of AI sovereignty has become an increasingly pertinent objective for nation-states and private companies developing, deploying, and operating systems critical to national security. AI sovereignty has become a prerequisite across product development life cycles. In this paper it is understood as a layered set of resources required to build and operate AI systems [1, 2]. Because these resources currently depend on infrastructure that can be geographically located and licensed, proposals to place data centers in orbit challenge sovereignty concepts that are typically grounded in territorial jurisdiction [3]. This paper explores the implications of pursuing AI sovereignty through the development of space-based data centers. In particular, it highlights the potential geopolitical challenges and risks posed by the pursuit of AI sovereignty in the space domain by examining defining geopolitical events that have shaped policies, technologies, and practices in the space sector: the Cold War space race, Europe’s development of its own Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS), the formation of International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR), and the U.S. Wolf Amendment of 2011. These events serve as analogies for examining how geopolitics and technology have shaped access, dependence, and concentration of sovereignty in the 21st century [4].</jats:p>
title: Space-based data centers and AI sovereignty

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In recent years, the rapid development of artificial intelligence has raised a series of ethical issues. How to balance AI innovation and AI governance has attracted wide attention from society. Some principle-based and practical approaches have already emerged. However, these strategies mainly face problems of time, speed, and cost. They fail to fundamentally balance dynamic factors and the need for explainability. This study proposes an explainable and adaptive AI governance approach from the perspective of time to balance AI governance and AI innovation. Causal models have causal explanation capabilities. They meet the requirements of responsible innovation. They can improve governance speed and reduce governance and innovation costs. Taking Bayesian networks as an example, they have explainability and dynamic adaptation ability. Bayesian networks can be used as a governance step before a regulatory sandbox. Bayesian networks can implement a human-assisted regulatory approach. This approach can combine the EU Artificial Intelligence Act with scholars’ recommendations on quantifiable risk levels. The explainable and adaptive AI governance approach has three important meanings for AI governance. First, it can provide an inclusive governance path. Second, it can supplement static governance strategies. Third, it can automatically generate explainable value alignment schemes.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>The paper provides an up-to-date overview of the data governance framework developed by the People’s Republic of China. The work investigates whether and how the domestic legal framework on data governance has influenced Chinese trade policy with reference to cross-border data flows and e-commerce issues (at the WTO and G20 level). This study shows that Chinese data governance features a two-pronged legal architecture in which the Cyberspace Administration of China plays a prominent role. By prioritizing the need to maintain party-state domestic control across the digital economy, China has proved to be extremely averse to any international agreement that could undermine its domestic data governance framework.</jats:p>
title: Chinese Data Governance and Trade Policy: From Cyber Sovereignty to the Quest for Digital Hegemony?

items.abstract: <jats:p>This research develops Constitutional Sovereignty Doctrine, or CSD, as a socio technical governance framework for assessing whether a public institution retains sufficient lawful, operational, computational, evidentiary, and remedial control over an AI-enabled decision system for which it remains legally and constitutionally accountable. The doctrine extends beyond territorial data residency and infrastructure ownership by examining control across the decision chain, including lawful authority, data, infrastructure, models and inference, human judgement, evidentiary traceability, rights and review, and corrective capacity. The paper also introduces Accountability-Control Asymmetry (ACA), a diagnostic concept describing situations in which formal responsibility remains with a public institution while the practical capabilities required to supervise, explain, reconstruct, intervene in, or remedy a decision are distributed elsewhere. CSD is grounded in Constitutional Intelligence, Canadian administrative law, contemporary digital-sovereignty policy, research on meaningful human oversight and procedural fairness, and international AI-governance standards. The eight dimensions are expressed through a functional model, CSD = f(A, D, I, M, J, E, R, C), and are treated as assessable institutional capabilities rather than as a predetermined numerical index. The research design therefore emphasises construct validity, expert assessment, architecture-based experiments, inter-rater reliability, and comparison with simpler sovereignty proxies such as data residency and infrastructure ownership.</jats:p>
title: Constitutional Sovereignty Doctrine: A Control-Based  Architecture for Trustworthy AI, Data Sovereignty, and  Accountable Digital Decision Systems

items.abstract: <jats:p>Oral traditions, ecological practices, and customary rules are all ingrained in the rich cultural history and knowledge systems of tribal societies. However, globalization, displacement, and a decline in intergenerational transmission are posing a growing danger to these knowledge systems. In order to overcome these obstacles, this study suggests a mobile framework powered by artificial intelligence (AI) that combines Geographic Information Systems (GIS), Natural Language Processing (NLP), Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), and Machine Translation (MT) for documentation and preservation. The methodology uses a mixed-methods approach, integrating AI-based simulations with ethnographic research. Audio-visual recordings of ecological wisdom and oral histories are made using mobile devices and annotated using Praat and ELAN. While NLP and MT use Marian NMT and Hugging Face models for translation (assessed using BLEU and METEOR), the ASR pipeline uses Kaldi, ESPnet, and wav2vec 2.0 for transcription (measured with Word Error Rate). Cultural and ecological sites are documented by GIS mapping using QGIS and ArcGIS. Data is kept in community-controlled Mukurtu archives, and ethical considerations are incorporated through Indigenous Data Sovereignty (IDS) and the CARE Principles. Initial results indicate 90% accuracy in GIS validation, BLEU scores ranging from 24 to 31, and WER between 18 and 22%. Although privacy concerns are raised, community surveys show that mobile-AI tools are well accepted (easy of use = 4.3/5). In addition to providing scalable technological solutions with policy importance in education, e-governance, and cultural sustainability, this study offers a socio-technical and ethical framework for the preservation of tribal knowledge.</jats:p>
title: AI-Driven Mobile Framework for Preserving Tribal Knowledge Systems Integration of ASR, NLP, and GIS under Data Sovereignty Principles

items.abstract: <jats:p>Data are becoming increasingly crucial to business and social digitalization, as such data have become a strategic asset that accelerates economic competitiveness and digitalization of society. In a societal context, it is important to maintain complete control over data, mainly once it is to be exchanged or shared. Another challenge is associated with who has control over data produced from digital platforms used by citizens. This ability is termed data sovereignty. Digital sovereignty refers to the concept of control, self-determination, and the ability of individuals or business entities to govern and exercise their right to utilize their data. As such, digital and data sovereignty is of paramount importance to enhance data usage and ownership policies. However, less attention has been given to exploring how digital sovereignty can be achieved by digital platforms used by citizens and what policies should be put in place to re-enforce the digital rights of citizens. Moreover, there are fewer guidelines on digital sovereignty requirements in the literature. This article employs qualitative review and comparative policy analysis of European Union (EU)–United States (US) digital initiatives to identify and aggregate policies aimed at providing a common understanding of digital and data sovereignty. This study contributes to addressing challenges faced by companies in implementing initiatives needed to ensure that the digital sovereignty of citizens is preserved when they use digital platforms. Findings from this study present key requirements (technical, legal–institutional, individual, infrastructural, and cross-cutting dimensions) and digital sovereignty initiatives that apply to citizens within the EU–US.</jats:p>
title: Digital and Data Sovereignty in Digital Platforms: Qualitative Review and Comparative Policy Analysis

items.abstract: <jats:p>This working paper develops the concept of control sovereignty as the next step in the legal and institutional theory of artificial intelligence. It builds on the thesis that advanced AI systems increasingly require machine-scale control architectures at the operational level, while normative, 2 constitutional and professional standards of control remain non-delegable to machines. The paper argues that democratic institutions face a double deficit. If they lack operational AI capability, they lose the capacity to act, learn, defend, administer and decide under conditions of machine-speed complexity. If they deploy AI systems without contestable legal control, they risk surrendering the conditions of human judgment, institutional accountability and democratic legitimacy. Control sovereignty is therefore defined as the institutional capacity to understand, procure, integrate, test, monitor, challenge, limit, replace and legally contest AI-based control infrastructures. Drawing on cybernetics, AI-control research, European and international AI governance instruments, riskmanagement frameworks and legal-AI evidence, the paper proposes a dual architecture: operational capability must pass a stress-condition capability test, and normative governance must pass a rule-oflaw contestability test. The central claim is that AI sovereignty cannot mean technological autarky, regulatory abstinence or uncritical adoption of powerful systems. It must mean contestable capability: the ability to use machine control without losing the institutional power to control the control of machines.</jats:p>
title: AI Sovereignty as Control Sovereignty

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
	  <jats:p>As data becomes a key component of urban governance, the night-time economy is still barely visible in datasets or in policies to improve urban life. In the last 20 years, over 50 cities worldwide appointed night mayors and governance mechanisms to tackle conflicts, foster innovation, and help the night-time economy sector grow. However, the intersection of data, digital rights, and 24-hour cities still needs more studies, examples, and policies. Here, the key argument is that the increasing importance of the urban night in academia and local governments claims for much-needed responsible data practices to support and protect nightlife ecosystems. By understanding these ecosystems and addressing data invisibilities, it is possible to develop a robust framework anchored in safeguarding human rights in the digital space and create comprehensive policies to help such ecosystems thrive. Night-time governance matters for the data policy community for three reasons. First, it brings together issues covered in different disciplines by various stakeholders. We need to build bridges between sectors to avoid siloed views of urban data governance. Second, thinking about data in cities also means considering the social, economic, and cultural impact of datafication and artificial intelligence on a 24-hour cycle. Creating a digital rights framework for the night means putting into practice principles of justice, ethics, and responsibility. Third, as Night Studies is an emerging field of research, policy and advocacy, there is an opportunity to help shape how, why, and when data about the night is collected and made available to society.</jats:p>
title: Invisible data in night-time governance: addressing policy gaps and building a digital rights framework for cities after dark

items.abstract: <jats:p>The article aims to clarify how digital sovereignty acquires new meanings within a technological environment shaped by distributed networks, decentralized infrastructures, and geopolitical pressures related to data control. In an era where data processing, storage, and transfer increasingly occur independently of the territorial space of states, and infrastructure providers operate transnationally, the traditional concept of sovereignty proves insufficient to reflect current realities. The article proposes a coherent interpretation of the relationships among the digital, cyber, and technological dimensions of sovereignty, highlighting how these aspects influence governance mechanisms, the distribution of control, and the ability of the actors involved - legal persons, public entities, and individuals - to understand and manage information flows. The analysis begins with a description of the transformations triggered by emerging technical infrastructures, particularly those associated with cloud computing, blockchain, and peer-to-peer networks. These technologies enhance operational flexibility but simultaneously introduce new levels of dependency, fragmentation, and opacity, which affect the possibility of exercising effective control over data. Against this backdrop, the article outlines the differences among the main consolidated normative models: the European approach, focused on protecting fundamental rights and mitigating power asymmetries between users and providers; the United States’ orientation, which privileges economic dynamism and innovation; and the regimes of states that value information control as a tool for reinforcing political authority. In its final part, the article discusses the challenges of assigning responsibility in decentralized technical environments, where reduced traceability and the absence of a single decision-making center complicate the application of existing legal norms. Digital sovereignty cannot be addressed through a single disciplinary lens and requires a shared understanding of the legal, technical, and geopolitical factors that shape the contemporary digital space. The article emphasizes that tensions among distributed infrastructures, global economic interests, and traditional forms of authority will continue to shape the debate on data control in the coming years.</jats:p>
title: DIGITAL SOVEREIGNTY IN THE CONTEXT OF DISTRIBUTED NETWORKS AND GLOBAL COMPETITION FOR DATA CONTROL

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The practice of public administration is confronted by an overwhelming volume of unstructured textual data, creating a critical bottleneck that challenges the capacity for timely, evidence-based policymaking. While large language models (LLMs) offer a powerful solution, the academic and policy discourse on AI governance has primarily focused on the risks associated with quantitative, predictive models, leaving the governance of LLMs, which involve qualitative, interpretive analysis, critically underexplored. This article provides a systematic and empirical answer to this challenge. We evaluate four distinct archetypes for AI-assisted policy analysis: (1) traditional expert-driven analysis, (2) automated topic modelling, (3) human-in-the-loop LLM co-production (ChatGPT with prompting), and (4) institutional-scale API automation (ChatGPT via API), by applying them to a real-world corpus of 63 United Nations policy documents. Our results reveal the inherent trade-offs of each archetype in terms of analytical speed, cost, contextual depth, and the requisite level of human oversight, finding that the human-in-the-loop model offers the most effective balance. We conclude by presenting a durable framework to guide public institutions in making a strategic, evidence-based choice of analytical workflow, ensuring the adoption of AI strengthens, rather than erodes, the integrity of democratic governance.</jats:p>
title: Governing the evidence base: An empirical framework of AI archetypes for policy analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
	  <jats:p>In our data-driven society, personal data affecting individuals as data subjects are increasingly being collected and processed by sizeable and international companies. While data protection laws and privacy technologies attempt to limit the impact of data breaches and privacy scandals, they rely on individuals having a detailed understanding of the available recourse, resulting in the responsibilization of data protection. Existing data stewardship frameworks incorporate data-protection-by-design principles but may not include data subjects in the data protection process itself, relying on supplementary legal doctrines to better enforce data protection regulations. To better protect individual autonomy over personal data, this paper proposes a data protection-focused data commons to encourage co-creation of data protection solutions and rebalance power between data subjects and data controllers. We conduct interviews with commons experts to identify the institutional barriers to creating a commons and challenges of incorporating data protection principles into a commons, encouraging participatory innovation in data governance. We find that working with stakeholders of different backgrounds can support a commons’ implementation by openly recognizing data protection limitations in laws, technologies, and policies when applied independently. We propose requirements for deploying a data protection-focused data commons by applying our findings and data protection principles such as purpose limitation and exercising data subject rights to the Institutional Analysis and Development (IAD) framework. Finally, we map the IAD framework into a commons checklist for policy-makers to accommodate co-creation and participation for all stakeholders, balancing the data protection of data subjects with opportunities for seeking value from personal data.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Bu çalışma, dijital dönüşümün kırsal kalkınma üzerindeki etkilerini kırsal dayanıklılık, yapay zeka destekli tarım, veri egemenliği ve dijital adalet konuları çerçevesinde kapsamlı bir şekilde incelemektedir. Kırsal dayanıklılığın yalnızca çevresel şoklara karşı teknik bir uyum kapasitesi değil; aynı zamanda sosyal, kurumsal ve dijital yönetişim süreçlerinin etkileşimiyle şekillenen çok boyutlu bir olgu olduğu ortaya konulmaktadır. Yapay zeka destekli dijital tarım uygulamaları, verimlilik, kaynakların etkin kullanımı ve iklim adaptasyonu açısından önemli avantajlar sunmaktadır. Ancak, bu potansiyelin topluma fayda sağlaması için veri sahipliği, şeffaflık ve kapsayıcı yönetim prensiplerinin benimsenmesi gerekmektedir. Araştırma, veri kooperatifleri ve toplum temelli veri yönetimi yöntemlerinin küçük üreticilerin dijital ekonomideki yerini güçlendirdiğini ve bilgi dengesizliklerini azalttığını ortaya koymaktadır. Bununla birlikte, dijital dönüşüm kırsal alanlarda altyapı, erişim, beceri ve güven gibi çok yönlü eşitsizlikler ortaya çıkarabilir. Bu sebeple dijital adalet ve altyapı adaleti, sürdürülebilir bir dijital gelişim için temel unsurlar olarak değerlendirilmelidir. Bu çalışma, kırsal dijital kapsayıcılığın sosyal adalet yönünü ele alıyor; özellikle kadınlar ve gençlerin dijital yetkinliklerinin artırılması, yaşam boyu öğrenme sistemleri ile cinsiyet odaklı politikaların önemini ön plana çıkarıyor. Sonuç olarak, dijital dönüşüm kırsal bölgelerde yalnızca bir teknolojik sorun değil; aynı zamanda haklara dayalı, katılımcı ve dayanışmacı bir kalkınma anlayışı olarak görülmelidir.</jats:p>
